newsitem.title: USA: Japanese keep auto productivity lead over Detroit.
newsitem.headline: Japanese keep auto productivity lead over Detroit.

text.p: Japanese automakers are maintaining a comfortable lead over their Detroit counterparts in North American productivity and are gaining in profitability, according to a widely watched manufacturing study released on Wednesday.

The 1997 Harbour Report, based on extensive studies of North American assembly, stamping, engine and transmission plants, underscores the pressure on General Motors Corp., Chrysler Corp. and Ford Motor Co. to build more vehicles with fewer workers.

For the fourth consecutive year, the Harbour Report rated Nissan Motor Co. Ltd the most efficient vehicle assembler in North America, with its giant Smyrna, Tenn., plant needing an average of 2.23 workers to build each vehicle, up from 2.09 a year ago.
Nissan also continued to lead in the key measure of overall labor productivity for stamping, powertrain and assembly operations, with 28.32 labor hours per vehicle.
Honda Motor Co. Ltd and Toyota Motor Corp also maintained their second- and third-place spots in the survey at 29.54 and 30.88 hours, respectively.
GM, Ford and Chrysler continued to make gains in labor productivity but remained at a significant cost disadvantage compared with Nissan.

The study estimated that GM, which requires 44.59 labor hours per vehicle, would be able to cut costs by $3.53 billion annually if it could reach Nissan's productivity levels, compared with $4.3 billion in last year's survey. But GM would have to shed 53,362 hourly workers to reach the Nissan benchmark.
Ford, which requires 37.59 hours per vehicle, would need to shed 21,062 workers and $1.7 billion in costs to reach Nissan's productivity level, compared with $1.9 billion in last year's survey.
Chrysler, needing 40.53 hours per vehicle, would need to cut 17,968 workers and $1.45 billion in costs, vs. $1.66 billion in last year's survey.

In recent years, the Big Three have outstripped Japanese automakers in profitability -- a result of their dominance in pickup trucks, sport utility vehicles and minivans -- but the Japanese are catching up, partly due to recent weakness of the yen vs. the dollar.

Chrysler earned $2,011 in pre-tax worldwide automotive profits per vehicle during the first quarter of 1997, compared with $949 for Ford and $843 for GM. In the fiscal year ended March 31, Toyota earned $1,425 per vehicle, up from $957 in fiscal 1996, while Honda earned $1,050, up from $182. Nissan, which lost money for the past four years, earned $450 per vehicle.
James Harbour, chairman of Harbour & Associates, said Japanese automakers will continue to improve in profitability as they bring out more light trucks and sport utility vehicles.

The study showed that the Big Three, despite stiff opposition to work force reductions from the United Auto Workers union, cannot afford to let up on their pursuit of productivity gains, Harbour said.
"General Motors hasn't got a choice. I don't think in some cases Chrysler has a choice either," Harbour said. "Everybody's going to have to compete in the world."
GM, suffering from a seven-week strike at its Pontiac, Mich., truck plant over UAW demands for more jobs, faces strike deadlines at three parts plants Thursday and Friday.
If those facilities in Wisconsin and Michigan strike, all of GM's North American assembly plants could shut down within days, costing the automaker hundreds of millions of dollars.

But even with their UAW contracts, GM, Ford and Chrysler will be able to make significant productivity gains on the Japanese by using more common vehicle components and designing cars and trucks for better manufacturing ease.

"I think General Motors can make some major strides to make themselves world-class from a cost-per-unit basis as they continue this approach to common systems and lean manufacturing," said Patricia Watters, Harbour's vice president of consulting. "GM has a horrendous amount of bad past to undo and bad practices to undo to get there."
